title: Slang: nightlife, drinking, romance, sex and drugs

blocks.title: Η νύχτα: βγαίνω, ξενυχτάω, το ξενύχτι
blocks.text:
Greek nightlife runs late and runs social. Dinner starts at 21:30 or 22:00, people meet for a drink around midnight, clubs and **μπουζούκια** fill after 01:00, and an **after** (after-hours bar) can keep going until the bakeries open. The vocabulary reflects that rhythm: the basic verb is simply **βγαίνω** (*I go out*), and the night itself is **η έξοδος** (*the night out*, also the neutral newspaper word) and the everyday report is simply *βγήκαμε χθες* (*we went out last night*).

**ξενυχτάω / ξενυχτώ** (*to stay up all night*, lit. *to un-night*) gives **το ξενύχτι** (*the all-nighter*), **ο ξενύχτης / η ξενύχτισσα** (*night owl, party animal*) and the adjective **ξενυχτισμένος** (*wrecked from no sleep*). It covers studying all night as well as partying, so context decides: *Ξενύχτησα για την εξέταση* (studied) vs *Ξενυχτήσαμε στα Γκάζι* (partied in Gazi).

The going-out routine has fixed collocations you should learn as chunks: **πάμε για ποτό;** (*shall we go for a drink?*), **βγαίνουμε για ποτάκι** (the diminutive makes it casual and harmless: *just one drink*, which is never true), **πάμε για χορό** (*dancing*), **πάμε για καφέ** (the daytime equivalent, and just as social), **τη βγάλαμε έξω** (*we took her out*, e.g. for her birthday), **γύρισα ξημερώματα** (*I came home at dawn*) and the proud boast **γύρισα με τον ήλιο** (*I got home with the sun up*).

Paying is its own vocabulary. **Κερνάω** (*I'm treating / it's on me*) is a social act, not just a transaction: whoever invited usually pays, and refusing to let someone treat you can come across as cold. **Κερνάει το μαγαζί** means *it's on the house*, and an unasked-for shot, fruit plate or dessert at the end of a meal is a **κέρασμα**. Splitting is **ρεφενές / πάμε ρεφενέ** (each person pays a share) or **τα σπάμε** (*we break it up*, i.e. split the bill), and the counter-move is **άσε, θα το πάρω εγώ** (*leave it, I'll get it*), followed by a ritual tug-of-war over the bill.

blocks.title: Μπουζούκια, πίστα, λουλούδια: what happens on a big night
blocks.text:
**Τα μπουζούκια** are a specifically Greek institution: a large club (often a converted warehouse, in summer an open-air venue by the sea) where a headline **λαϊκός τραγουδιστής** sings live with a band until four or five in the morning. You **κλείνεις τραπέζι** in advance, the table comes with a minimum (usually a bottle of whisky or vodka with mixers and fruit), and the closer you sit to **την πίστα**, the more you pay. When a song hits, people climb onto the πίστα (or on the table) to dance a **ζεϊμπέκικο** or **τσιφτετέλι**.

**Τα πιάτα.** The famous plate-smashing has a precise history: it was associated with the bouzouki clubs of the 1950s-60s and spread internationally through the film *Ποτέ την Κυριακή* (1960). The military regime **banned plate-smashing in nightclubs in 1969** because flying shards injured people, and it is still not allowed in clubs. Some places sell plaster plates for weddings or tourists, but in a modern μπουζούκια the gesture of extravagance is **λουλούδια**.

**Τα λουλούδια.** A waiter walks around with **πανέρια** or **δίσκους** (baskets, trays) of carnation or rose petals, and customers buy them to shower the singer or someone dancing. **Του έριξαν λουλούδια** (*they showered him with flowers*) is a compliment; buying many trays is a public display of money and κέφι, and photos of singers buried in flowers regularly cause online debate about waste. The verb is **ρίχνω λουλούδια** (*to throw flowers*).

**Το σκυλάδικο** is the snob's word for the down-market version: the suffix -άδικο (cf. *ψαράδικο* fishmonger's, *ρεμπετάδικο*) plus σκύλος evokes howling dogs. People use it ironically about places they secretly love (*πάμε σε κανένα σκυλάδικο να ξεσκάσουμε*), and **σκυλάδικο τραγούδι / σκυλάδικα** for the music: dramatic, heartbroken, sung by a **καψούρης** (see below).

**Κέφι** is the key concept: the high spirits that make a night. **Έχω κέφια** (*I'm in a great mood*), **μου 'φυγε το κέφι** (*I lost my mood*), **κεφάτος** (*in good spirits*), and the ultimate verdict: **γινόταν χαμός** (*it was mayhem, it was amazing*).

blocks.title: Drinking: the verbs
blocks.text:
**Μεθάω / μεθώ** (aorist **μέθυσα**, participle **μεθυσμένος**) is both intransitive (*I get drunk*) and transitive (*I get someone drunk*: *Μας μέθυσε με τα τσίπουρα*). The noun is **το μεθύσι** (*drunkenness, the state*), and **η μέθη** is the formal/legal word (*οδήγηση υπό την επήρεια μέθης*). A heavy drinker is **ο μπεκρής** (pejorative, Turkish loan; *μπεκρού* for a woman is rare and very pejorative) or **ο μεθύστακας**; a gentler way is **του αρέσει το ποτό** or **τα τσούζει** (*he hits the bottle*, lit. *it stings them*).

**Πιωμένος** (*having drunk, under the influence*) is the neutral adjective, and **ψιλοπιωμένος** (with the prefix ψιλο- *slightly*) is *tipsy*. **Ζαλισμένος** literally means *dizzy* and is the usual soft word for *a bit drunk*: *Είμαι λίγο ζαλισμένος, δεν οδηγώ.* To sober up is **ξεμεθάω** or **ξενερώνω** (the original meaning of ξενερώνω is *to sober up*; it later came to mean *to lose your buzz or mood*, and that figurative sense is now the more common one).

Intensity is expressed by a big family of **expressive nouns used as predicates**: *είμαι λιώμα* (*I'm mush*), *έγινε στουπί* (*he became oakum*), *ήταν τύφλα* (*she was blindness*). Most of them can take the frame **... στο μεθύσι** (*... in drunkenness*), which makes clear you mean alcohol and not tiredness: **τύφλα στο μεθύσι, σκνίπα στο μεθύσι, τάβλα στο μεθύσι, στουπί στο μεθύσι**. Without that frame, **λιώμα, χάλια, πτώμα** can also mean *exhausted*.

blocks.title: Flirting and romance: the moves
blocks.text:
Greek has a rich vocabulary for each stage of attraction, and much of it is everyday colloquial rather than slang, so you will hear it from people of every age.

**Noticing.** **Μου αρέσει** (*I like him/her*) is neutral. **Μου κάνει** (*he/she suits me, is my type*: *Δεν μου κάνει ο τύπος*) and **μου κάνει κλικ** (*I click with him*) are casual. **Γουστάρω** (from Italian *gustare*) is more slangy and more physical: *Τη γουστάρω τρελά* = *I'm crazy about her / I really fancy her*. With things it just means *I'm into it* (*γουστάρω αυτό το μαγαζί*).

**Making a move.** **Την πέφτω σε κάποιον** (*I fall on someone*) = *to hit on someone*, and it is the core phrase: *Μου την έπεσε στο μπαρ* (*he hit on me at the bar*). **Φλερτάρω** is the neutral word (*to flirt*), with **το φλερτ**. **Ψήνω κάποιον** (*I bake someone*) = *to talk someone round, to win them over*: *Την ψήνω εδώ και ένα μήνα* (*I've been working on her for a month*); the passive **ψήνεται** = *(s)he's warming to it, is up for it*. **Κάνω καμάκι** (*I harpoon*) is the classic Greek pick-up, especially of tourists (see culture), and **καμάκι** is also the man who does it.

**Results.** If it works: **βγαίνουμε** (*we go on dates*), **τα φτιάξαμε** (*we got together*, lit. *we fixed them*), **τα 'χουμε** (*we're an item*), **είμαστε μαζί** (*we're together*, neutral). If it doesn't: **μου έριξε χυλόπιτα** (*(s)he turned me down*, lit. *threw me a noodle-pie*) and from the rejected person's side **έφαγα χυλόπιτα** (*I got knocked back*). **Με έστησε** = *(s)he stood me up* (στήνω = to make wait, to leave standing).

**Obsession.** **Η καψούρα** (from κάψα *burning heat*) is a hopeless, burning infatuation, and **καψουρεύομαι** (aorist **καψουρεύτηκα**) is *to fall hard*. The lovesick person is **ο καψούρης**, the songs are **καψουροτράγουδα**. **Έχω κόλλημα με κάποιον/κάτι** (*I'm stuck on*) is a fixation: a crush you can't shake, but also any obsession (*έχω κόλλημα με τα παπούτσια*). **Η καβάτζα** (*a stash, a backup*) is used for a person kept in reserve, the fallback you text when lonely.

**Endings.** **Χωρίζω** (*to break up*; *χωρίσαμε*) is neutral. **Τα χαλάσαμε** (*we broke them*) is colloquial for a break-up or a falling-out. **Με κεράτωσε** (*(s)he cheated on me*), from **κέρατο** (*horn*): the cheated partner is said to wear horns, **φοράει κέρατα**, and **ο κερατάς** is the cuckold (insulting, 3; between friends also *you rascal*). **Μου την έφερε** (*(s)he tricked me, played me*) and **με παράτησε** (*(s)he dumped me*) round out the vocabulary of misery.

blocks.title: Καμάκι, καψούρα και η ελληνική παρέα
blocks.text:
**Το καμάκι.** In the 1970s and 1980s, the boom in mass tourism produced a famous Greek type: the **καμάκι**, a young man who spent the summer chasing Scandinavian, British and German tourists on the islands and in Athens. The word is the fisherman's harpoon (from ancient *κάμαξ* 'pole'), and the image was a hunter spearing fish. The stock figure wore open shirts, bell-bottoms and big belt buckles, danced, flattered and promised love in broken English. Vasilis Vasilikos wrote a book called *Τα καμάκια* (1978), and in the 1980s feminists criticised the culture. Today **κάνω καμάκι** is used jokingly for any obvious, persistent chat-up: *Σταμάτα το καμάκι στη σερβιτόρα.*

**Η καψούρα** is close to a national genre. Whole sub-genres of λαϊκά and σκυλάδικα are **καψουροτράγουδα**, songs of humiliating, wine-soaked love, and the drunk καψούρης crying into his whisky while the singer sings *his* song is a recognised character. Friends will diagnose you: *Είσαι σε φάση καψούρας* (*you're in a lovesick phase*).

**Η παρέα.** Greeks go out in groups much more than in pairs. Flirting often happens inside or between παρέες, and an introduction by a mutual friend is valued. Going out alone to a bar is unusual. The flip side: a group will notice, comment on and tease any flirtation instantly. **Ποιος είναι αυτός;** (*who's that guy?*) from your friends is not an idle question.

**Τα κέρατα.** Horns as the sign of the cuckold are pan-Mediterranean. In Greece the topic is a rich source of jokes and insults, and the gesture (index and little finger raised) is offensive. **Του φόρεσε κέρατα** = *she cheated on him*.

blocks.title: Sex: the register ladder
blocks.text:
For sex Greek has a clear ladder from clinical to obscene, and the rung you pick says a lot about you and the situation. Learn to **recognise** everything, and **produce** only the first few rungs until you know the people well.

**Formal/clinical:** **η σεξουαλική επαφή** (*sexual intercourse*), **η συνουσία** (*coitus*, very learned), **έχω σεξουαλικές σχέσεις με** (*to have sexual relations with*). Doctors, news, legal texts.

**Neutral and polite:** **κάνω έρωτα** (*to make love*: tender, a bit romantic), **κάνω σεξ** (*to have sex*: neutral, direct, the everyday adult word), **κοιμάμαι με κάποιον** (*to sleep with*, euphemism as in English), **το κάναμε** (*we did it*: coy, teenage). **Πάω με κάποιον** (*I go with someone*) is a casual, slightly crude euphemism for *to sleep with*, often used about one-off sex or about sex workers: *Πήγε με την πρώτη που βρήκε*.

**Vulgar:** **πηδάω** (*to jump* → *to fuck, to shag*, 4), passive/reciprocal **πηδιέμαι** (*πηδιόντουσαν όλο το βράδυ*), noun **το πήδημα** (*a shag; also figuratively a rip-off*: *Τι πήδημα ήταν αυτός ο λογαριασμός!*). **Γαμάω / γαμώ** (*to fuck*, 5) is the strongest literal verb, and its huge family of curses (*γαμώτο, άντε γαμήσου, τη γάμησα*) belongs to the swearing unit; in the literal sexual sense it is coarser than πηδάω and very much locker-room language. **Ο γάμος** (*marriage*) shares the root, which is a source of endless puns.

**Desire.** **Η καύλα** (*horniness; an erection*) and **καυλώνω** (*to get horny / to turn someone on*) are vulgar (4), and **καυλωμένος / καυλιάρης** (*horny / a horndog*) likewise. But like English *horny* or *stoked*, the family has escaped into general slang: **η καύλα** can mean an intense sudden urge for anything (*μου 'ρθε μια καύλα για σουβλάκι*), and **ξεκαυλώνω** (*to lose one's arousal*) is used figuratively for *to lose enthusiasm, to have one's buzz killed*: *Μόλις είδα τις τιμές, ξεκαύλωσα* (*as soon as I saw the prices, I lost interest*). It is still rude (3-4): the polite equivalent is **ξενερώνω** (*Μόλις είδα τις τιμές, ξενέρωσα*), which is what you should actually say.

**Masturbation.** Polite: **αυτοϊκανοποιούμαι / η αυτοϊκανοποίηση** (*self-satisfaction*: the word is literally also used for complacency). Clinical: **ο αυνανισμός**. Vulgar: **η μαλακία** (4 in this literal sense) and **τον παίζω** (*I play with it*, male, 4). The literal meaning of μαλακία is why **μαλάκας** is an insult (*wanker*) and why **μαλακίες** means *bullshit, nonsense*: that whole family is covered in the swearing unit.

**το πουλί / πουλάκι** (little bird: children and euphemism)
**4-5**: πούτσος 4-5, ψωλή 5 (often 'erect penis'); used in curses (*στον πούτσο μου* = I don't give a damn)
no neutral everyday word: people use the medical word or circumlocute (*εκεί κάτω*)
**5**: taboo; also used to call a woman attractive (objectifying), a mess (*έγινε μουνί*), or a nasty person
**4**; heavily idiomatic: *αρχίδια!* = bullshit!, *τα 'κανε αρχίδια* = he screwed it up; see swearing unit

blocks.text:
**Where these words actually live**

Greek is famously relaxed about strong language among friends: a group of thirty-somethings at a taverna may say *μαλάκα* every other sentence and joke about who **πήδηξε** whom. But the line is sharp at the edge of the παρέα. With someone's parents, a new colleague, a doctor, a teacher or a date you have just met, use the first column: **κάνω σεξ / κοιμάμαι με / στήθος / πισινός**. The body words at 4-5 (**μουνί, ψωλή, πούτσος**) said *to* a woman you don't know are sexual harassment, not banter. Women swear too, and plenty of Greek women use **γαμώτο** and **μαλακίες** freely, but a man using sexual vocabulary *about* a woman to strangers is judged harshly. As a foreigner, under-shooting by one notch on the scale is always safer than over-shooting.

blocks.title: Drugs: words, register, reality
blocks.text:
Drug vocabulary in Greek comes in layers: official words from the news and the law, slang from users and the street, and an older layer from the **rebetiko** subculture of the 1920s-30s.

**Cannabis.** The official word is **η κάνναβη** (and **η μαριχουάνα, το χασίς/χασίσι** for the products). The slang for the weed itself is **το χόρτο** (*grass*, exactly as in English), and a joint is **ο μπάφος** (from the onomatopoeia of a puff, *μπαφ*) or **το τσιγαριλίκι** (old-school, with Turkish -λίκι), and with older or rebetiko-minded people **το γάρο**. **Το στριφτό** (*the rolled one*) is a hand-rolled cigarette, tobacco only; you'll hear *στρίβω ένα* (*I roll one*) about both. **Φουμάρω** (*to smoke*, Italian *fumare*) is slangy for smoking weed.

**Being high.** **Η μαστούρα** is *the high* (and, with the article, a user), **μαστουρώνω** is *to get high*, **μαστουρωμένος** = *stoned*. **Φτιάχνομαι** (*I get made*) = *I get high*, and **φτιαγμένος** = *high*: a classic false friend, since **φτιαγμένος** in its normal meaning just means *made, fixed*. Context: *Ήταν φτιαγμένος, γελούσε μόνος του.* **Ξενερώνω** (again) = *to come down / sober up*.

**Harder drugs.** **Η πρέζα** is from Italian *presa* (*a pinch*: still the normal word for *a pinch of salt*), and became slang for a dose of snorted powder, then specifically **heroin**. **Ο πρεζάκιας** (*junkie*, 3, contemptuous) and **το πρεζόνι** (*junkie*, harsher, 3-4) are its derivatives. **Η σκόνη** (*dust, powder*) and **η κόκα** are slang for cocaine (**η κοκαΐνη** officially); **το χάπι / τα χάπια** (*the pill(s)*) means ecstasy/MDMA in party talk, though it is also the normal word for any tablet, so **πήρε χάπι** needs context. **Ο ντίλερ** is the dealer; **η δόση** is a dose/fix.

**Register.** Using this vocabulary is not shocking in itself: news reports, films and songs are full of it, and **μπάφος** or **μαστούρα** are casual slang (2), not swearwords. **Πρεζάκιας / πρεζόνι** are stigmatising insults and should not be used about real people with addiction problems; the respectful term is **χρήστης (ουσιών)** or **εξαρτημένος**.

blocks.title: Από τον τεκέ στο σήμερα: rebetiko and the law
blocks.text:
**Rebetiko.** The urban music of the refugees and the underclass of Piraeus, Thessaloniki and Athens grew up partly in **τεκέδες**, hashish dens with water pipes (**ναργιλέδες**), where the **μάγκες** smoked and played bouzouki and baglamas. Rebetiko scholar Ilias Petropoulos famously described the prison and the hash den as the womb of the genre. Songs about hashish are called **χασικλίδικα**, and some songs also mention cocaine and **πρέζα**, although such songs are a small minority of the repertoire. The **Metaxas dictatorship closed the τεκέδες in 1936-37** and censored lyrics from 1937, so drug references vanished from records; censorship laws on songs were formally abolished only in 1981. The mangas vocabulary of the period (μάγκας, μόρτης, τεκές, μαστούρης) is covered further in the regional/rebetiko unit.

**The law today.** Cannabis is legal in Greece **only for medical use** (authorised in 2017, prescription-based); recreational possession remains a criminal offence, with possession for personal use treated as a misdemeanour (usually ending in a suspended sentence or diversion) and supply treated severely. Rules on CBD and low-THC products have changed several times, so do not assume that a shop selling 'κάνναβη' is legal. Practically: drug talk is common and casual among young people, but using drugs openly in public is not, and police checks at festivals and islands happen.

**Alcohol culture.** Greeks drink a lot socially but **getting visibly drunk in public is frowned on** more than in northern Europe: alcohol is supposed to come with food (meze) and κέφι, not with collapse. The tourist drunk on the party islands is a stock figure of contempt. The **drink-drive limit is 0.5 g/l** (0.2 for new drivers and professionals), and the vocabulary *αλκοτέστ* (breathalyser test) is everyday.

blocks.title: Pronunciation notes
items: **μπ, γκ at the start of a word = [b], [g]**: μπαράκι [baˈɾaci], μπάφος [ˈbafos], μπουζούκια [buˈzuca], γκόμενα [ˈgomena]. Inside words they are often [mb], [ŋg] in careful speech, but many speakers say plain [b], [g] everywhere: *καμπάνα* [kaˈbana].

**υγειά vs υγεία.** The toast is **στην υγειά μας** with stress on the last syllable and a [ʝ] glide: [stin iˈʝa mas]. The dictionary noun **υγεία** (*health*) is [iˈʝia], three syllables. **Γεια μας** is [ʝa mas], one syllable for γεια.

**αυ before voiced consonants = [av]**: καύλα [ˈkavla], ξεκαυλώνω [ksekavˈlono]. Before voiceless ones it is [af]: *αυτοϊκανοποίηση* [aftoikanoˈpiisi], where the diaeresis on ϊ marks a separate vowel, not a diphthong.
**Elision is the norm in this register**: τα 'χουμε (τα έχουμε), μου 'ριξε (μου έριξε), μου 'χει ανέβει, να 'μαστε καλά, μου 'ρθε. Run the words together: [taˈxume], [muˈɾikse].

**Stress pairs to watch**: ξενυχτάω [ksenixˈtao] but ξενύχτι [kseˈnixti]; μεθάω [meˈθao] but μέθυσα [ˈmeθisa]; καψούρα [kaˈpsura] vs καψουρεύομαι [kapsuˈrevome]; σκυλάδικο [skiˈlaðiko], stress on -λά-; τύφλα on the first syllable, στουπί on the last.
**Emphatic lengthening**: for exaggeration Greeks stretch the stressed vowel and lean on it: *ήμουν λιιιώμα*, *τύυυφλα*, *ήταν τέλειοοο*. In writing (texts, chats) this appears as repeated letters.
**Intonation of teasing questions**: *Και; Φιληθήκατε;* rises steeply on the last stressed syllable; *Άντε!* (go on / no way) falls sharply. **Ωχ** is drawn out and falling for dismay.
**Πηδάω**: the aorist is **πήδηξα** (also πήδησα); in the vulgar sense both are heard. Present **πηδάω** and **πηδώ** both exist; the -άω form is more colloquial.

blocks.text:
**Common mistakes and false friends**

- **πηδάω** = *to jump* AND *to fuck*. *Πήδηξα το φράχτη* (fence) is fine, but *Θέλω να σε πηδήξω* is not a children's game. With a person as object it is always the vulgar sense.
- **φτιαγμένος** = *made, fixed* AND *high*. *Η πίτα είναι φτιαγμένη από τη γιαγιά* vs *Είναι φτιαγμένος* (about a person at a party).
- **πίτα, φέσι, τάβλα, στουπί** are normal nouns (*pie, fez, board, oakum*) that mean *drunk* only as predicates about people.
- **τύφλα να 'χει** is praise, not drunkenness: *Τύφλα να 'χει ο Τσιτσάνης* = *Tsitsanis has nothing on him*.
- **χόρτα** (plural) at a taverna are boiled wild greens; **χόρτο** (singular, in the right context) is weed.
- **σκόνη** is primarily *dust*. *Έχει σκόνη στο τραπέζι* is about cleaning.
- **η κόκα** is also *a Coca-Cola*: *Μια κόκα, παρακαλώ* in a café is innocent.
- **το χάπι** is any pill; *πήρα ένα χάπι για τον πονοκέφαλο* is aspirin.
- **ραντεβού** is any appointment (doctor, bank); it is a *date* only from context.
- **γκόμενα** is not a neutral word for girlfriend: in front of her parents say **η κοπέλα μου** (and **ο φίλος μου / το αγόρι μου** for a boyfriend).
- **κάνω έρωτα** is not *I fall in love* (that is **ερωτεύομαι**).
- **μου κάνει** also means *it fits me* (clothes): *Δεν μου κάνει το παντελόνι.*
- **ξενερώνω** is safe; **ξεκαυλώνω** is not, even though people use it figuratively.
- **καψούρα** is not *love* in general: it is hopeless, burning infatuation, often unrequited.

blocks.title: Σάββατο βράδυ: «ένα ποτάκι μόνο»
blocks.text:
Ρε παιδιά, πρέπει να σας πω τι έγινε το Σάββατο, γιατί ακόμα δεν έχω συνέλθει.

Ξεκινήσαμε αθώα. Ο Στέλιος είπε «πάμε για ένα ποτάκι», και ήμασταν πέντε άτομα σε ένα μπαράκι στο Κουκάκι. Ένα ποτάκι έγιναν τρία, και κάποια στιγμή ο Στέλιος, που κερνούσε σφηνάκια σαν να μην υπάρχει αύριο, ήταν ήδη φέσι. Η Δανάη είχε κόλλημα να πάμε μπουζούκια, γιατί τραγουδούσε ένας που γουστάρει τρελά. Εγώ είπα όχι, ότι δεν έχει ξενύχτι, ότι είμαι πτώμα από τη βδομάδα. Φυσικά στη μία ήμασταν στο τραπέζι, δίπλα στην πίστα, με ένα μπουκάλι ουίσκι που κόστιζε όσο το νοίκι μου.

Ο τραγουδιστής ξεκίνησε τα καψουροτράγουδα και η Δανάη ανέβηκε στην πίστα. Ο Στέλιος αγόρασε δύο πανέρια λουλούδια και της τα έριξε, ενώ εκείνη χόρευε ζεϊμπέκικο. Τότε εμφανίστηκε ένας τύπος από το διπλανό τραπέζι και μου την έπεσε. Ήταν συμπαθητικός, για να λέμε την αλήθεια μου έκανε κλικ. Με κέρασε ένα ποτό, μιλήσαμε, γελάσαμε, και κάπου εκεί φασωθήκαμε στο μπαλκόνι.

Μετά από μισή ώρα έρχεται μια κοπέλα και του λέει «αγάπη μου, πάμε;». Η γκόμενά του. Που καθόταν στο ίδιο τραπέζι. Εγώ ήμουν σίγουρα η καβάτζα της βραδιάς. Ξενέρωσα τελείως, πήγα στο μπαρ και παρήγγειλα κι άλλο σφηνάκι.

Στις πέντε ο Στέλιος ήταν τάβλα στο μεθύσι, η Δανάη είχε καψουρευτεί τον μπουζουξή, και εγώ ήμουν λιώμα. Πήγαμε σε ένα after στο Γκάζι, γιατί εμείς οι Έλληνες δεν ξέρουμε πότε να σταματήσουμε. Γύρισα σπίτι με τον ήλιο.

Την Κυριακή ξύπνησα στις δύο το μεσημέρι με ένα κεφάλι καζάνι και τρομερό χανγκόβερ. Στο κινητό είχα δεκαπέντε μηνύματα. Ο Στέλιος: «Ζεις;». Η Δανάη: «Μου έριξε χυλόπιτα ο μπουζουξής, αλλά τον έψησα να βγούμε την Πέμπτη!». Κι ένα από άγνωστο αριθμό: «Συγγνώμη για χθες. Χωρίσαμε. Πάμε για ποτό;».

Λοιπόν, παιδιά. Ορκίζομαι ότι δεν ξαναπίνω. Τουλάχιστον μέχρι το επόμενο Σάββατο. Εσείς τι λέτε, να του απαντήσω;
blocks.en:
Guys, I have to tell you what happened on Saturday, because I still haven't recovered.

We started innocently. Stelios said 'let's go for a quick drink', and there were five of us in a little bar in Koukaki. One quick drink became three, and at some point Stelios, who was buying shots as if there were no tomorrow, was already drunk. Danai was fixated on going to the bouzoukia, because a singer she's crazy about was on. I said no, that there'd be no all-nighter, that I was wrecked from the week. Of course at one o'clock we were at a table next to the dance floor, with a bottle of whisky that cost as much as my rent.

The singer started the lovesick songs and Danai got up on the dance floor. Stelios bought two baskets of flowers and threw them over her while she danced a zeibekiko. Then a guy from the next table appeared and hit on me. He was nice, to tell the truth I kind of clicked with him. He bought me a drink, we talked, we laughed, and somewhere around then we made out on the balcony.

Half an hour later a girl comes over and says to him 'darling, shall we go?'. His girlfriend. Who was sitting at the same table. I was definitely the evening's backup. I completely lost interest, went to the bar and ordered another shot.

At five Stelios was dead drunk, Danai had fallen hard for the bouzouki player, and I was wasted. We went to an after-hours place in Gazi, because we Greeks don't know when to stop. I got home with the sun up.

On Sunday I woke up at two in the afternoon with a pounding head and a terrible hangover. I had fifteen messages on my phone. Stelios: 'Are you alive?'. Danai: 'The bouzouki player turned me down, but I talked him into going out on Thursday!'. And one from an unknown number: 'Sorry about last night. We broke up. Shall we go for a drink?'.

So, guys. I swear I'm never drinking again. At least until next Saturday. What do you say, should I answer him?

items.prompt: Shall we go for a drink? (standard invitation)
items.why: πάμε για + accusative noun is the standard invitation; the diminutive ποτάκι makes it lighter.

items.prompt: It's on me! (I'm paying for the drinks)
items.why: κερνάω/κερνώ = to treat; the emphatic pronoun εγώ goes after the verb.

items.prompt: Cheers! (shortest toast, 'our health')
items.why: Γεια μας is the everyday toast; στην υγειά μας is the full form.

items.prompt: Bottoms up! (lit. 'white bottom')
items.why: Drain the glass until its (white) bottom shows.

items.prompt: I stayed up all night. (aorist of ξενυχτάω)
items.why: ξενυχτάω/ξενυχτώ → aorist ξενύχτησα, stress moves to -νύ-.

items.prompt: We got home at sunrise. (lit. 'with the sun')
items.why: Fixed boasting phrase; ξημερώματα = at dawn is also fine.

items.prompt: Let's split the bill (two colloquial ways: 'we break them' or 'Dutch').
items.why: τα σπάμε = split the bill; ρεφενές = each pays a share.

items.prompt: Say it politely, e.g. to your boss: «Ήμουν λιώμα χθες.»
items.why: ζαλισμένος (dizzy) is the soft word; λιώμα is slangy and exaggerated.

items.prompt: Make it stronger (colloquial): «Ήταν πολύ μεθυσμένος.» Use the 'blindness' word plus «στο μεθύσι».
items.why: τύφλα (στο μεθύσι) = blind drunk.

items.prompt: We got hammered (lit. we became oakum).
items.why: γίνομαι στουπί (στο μεθύσι) = to get hammered.

items.prompt: I'm a bit tipsy (use the prefix 'slightly').
items.why: ψιλο- + πιωμένος = tipsy.

items.prompt: The wine has gone to my head. (μου 'χει ...)
items.why: ανεβαίνω (to go up) + elided μου 'χει.

items.prompt: He hit on me at the bar.
items.why: την πέφτω σε κάποιον; with a weak pronoun: μου την έπεσε.

items.prompt: She turned me down. (lit. threw me a noodle-pie)
items.why: ρίχνω χυλόπιτα = to reject romantically.

items.prompt: I got knocked back. (from the rejected person's side: 'I ate...')
items.why: τρώω χυλόπιτα = to be turned down.

items.prompt: They got together in the summer. (lit. they fixed them)
items.why: τα φτιάχνω με κάποιον = to start a relationship.

items.prompt: I've fallen hard for him (I'm infatuated). One verb, aorist.
items.why: καψουρεύομαι, from καψούρα (burning crush).

items.prompt: She has a fixation on him / a crush she can't shake. (έχει ...)
items.why: έχω κόλλημα με/μαζί = to be fixated on.

items.prompt: He cheated on her. (verb from 'horn')
items.why: κερατώνω = to cheat on.

items.prompt: She stood me up for half an hour.
items.why: στήνω κάποιον = to keep someone waiting / stand them up.

items.prompt: I'm just his backup option. (the 'stash' word)
items.why: καβάτζα = reserve, backup partner.

items.prompt: Say this politely: «Μόλις είδα τις τιμές, ξεκαύλωσα.»
items.why: ξενερώνω is the clean equivalent of the vulgar ξεκαυλώνω (lose enthusiasm).

items.prompt: Say this neutrally (adult, not vulgar): «Πηδιούνται εδώ και μήνες.»
items.why: κάνω σεξ / κοιμάμαι με are neutral; πηδιέμαι is vulgar (4).

items.prompt: What's the polite/medical word for 'breasts' (sing., collective)?
items.why: βυζιά is crude (3); στήθος is neutral.

items.prompt: He was high (the slang participle meaning 'made').
items.why: φτιαγμένος = high; also μαστουρωμένος = stoned.

items.prompt: Roll a joint. (imperative + the 'puff' word)
items.why: στρίβω (aorist έστριψα) + μπάφος.

items.prompt: Heroin, slang (originally 'a pinch', from Italian).
items.why: Italian presa 'pinch' → dose → heroin.

items.prompt: I woke up with a pounding head (a 'cauldron').
items.why: κεφάλι καζάνι = pounding headache.

items.prompt: I made a total fool of myself. (became a laughing-stock)
items.why: γίνομαι ρεζίλι = to embarrass oneself.

items.prompt: We got turned away at the club door. (lit. we ate door)
